title: Crowd Science Overview
description: Crowd science is the study of how large numbers of people move, gather and behave in shared spaces, using density, flow, speed and space as its measured quantities, and it is the science behind safe planning for gatherings of millions. In Mecca it applies to ordinary city crowds, to pilgrimage movements between the Grand Mosque, Mina, Muzdalifah and Arafat, and to transport interchanges where rail, bus and foot flows meet. The field distinguishes a crowd that is dense but moving, which can be safe, from a crowd that is dense and stopped, which can become dangerous, and it treats design, scheduling, signage, staffing and monitoring as a single system, because a wide corridor with a bad schedule can fail as surely as a narrow one. This record is a model-based science record: its formulas are models of crowd behaviour, clearly labeled as models, and they are not records of any real event. Religious meanings of the movements studied are a matter of Islamic tradition, stated separately from the engineering facts. The demo below states the three core quantities of crowd science and their units, as the vocabulary every later record uses.

title: Density and Flow Fundamentals
description: Density is people per square metre, flow is people passing a line per unit time, and speed is distance per unit time, and the fundamental relationship used in crowd models is that flow through a width equals density multiplied by speed multiplied by that width, up to the point where rising density slows speed. At low density people walk near their free speed, about 1.3 metres per second in published pedestrian models; as density rises toward two people per square metre, speed falls; above about four people per square metre, movement becomes difficult and dangerous, and published crowd-safety guidance treats sustained densities in that range as a stop condition, not a design target. These thresholds are model guidance from published crowd science, not measurements from any particular Mecca event, and they vary with age, mobility, luggage, heat and slope. Flow capacity therefore has a peak: widening a corridor helps only until the downstream exit or the next bottleneck limits flow, which is why bottleneck analysis is a separate record in this pair. The demo below computes flow at three densities with falling speed, showing the peak and the fall, which is the central lesson of crowd flow.

title: Tawaf Crowd Dynamics (Published Studies and Models)
description: Tawaf is the ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba in the Grand Mosque, a movement held in Islamic tradition, and its crowd dynamics are studied in published models because thousands of people move in the same rotational direction around a centre at the same time. Published studies and models describe counterflow at entries and exits, faster inner lanes and slower outer lanes, congestion where flows join from gates, and the effect of the mosque's multiple levels, which separate some flows vertically. Where a published study gives a measured density or flow, this record treats it as a study result with its date and method; where this record gives numbers, they come from the general density-flow model in the previous record and are labeled as models, not as measurements from any particular pilgrimage. The ritual meaning of Tawaf is tradition, and the movement engineering is fact, and the two are kept apart throughout. No image, diagram or description of any person is used to illustrate this record. The demo below models an annulus, a ring, of walkers: its area from inner and outer radius, and the people it holds at a stated density, as a model of a circumambulation floor.

title: Jamarat Bridge Engineering and Crowd Safety
description: The Jamarat Bridge in Mina is a multi-level structure built to carry pilgrims performing the stoning ritual, a rite held in Islamic tradition, and its engineering is a published case study in crowd safety by design. The present bridge replaced earlier single-level arrangements with multiple levels, one-way flows, separated entry and exit routes, ramps, and large open decks, so that crowds arriving, performing the rite and leaving do not cross each other at the same points. Published design reporting describes the bridge as designed for very large hourly flows, with pillars, ventilation and emergency access built into the structure, and with scheduling by group and time as part of its operation. This record gives no hourly capacity as a verified current figure, because published design figures and operational figures differ by year and by level, and it treats the bridge as a system of structure plus schedule plus staffing, not as concrete alone. The ritual meaning is tradition; the structure and flows are engineering fact. The demo below models multi-level throughput as levels multiplied by per-level flow, showing why levels multiply capacity only if entries and exits also multiply.

title: Mina Tent-City Logistics
description: Mina is a tent city used during Hajj, where pilgrims stay in organised tent districts between movements to and from the other holy sites, and its logistics are a published case study in temporary-city planning. Tents are grouped by country and group, with fire-resistant materials, ventilation, air-conditioning in modern tents, water, sanitation, catering, medical posts and access roads, and the whole city operates for only a few days each year, which makes its logistics a build-operate-remove cycle rather than an ordinary city service. Movement in Mina is scheduled by group and route, so that tent districts empty and fill in waves rather than all at once, and the metro, buses and foot routes are planned against those waves. Fire safety, heat management and sanitation are the standing logistics risks, and published reporting describes drills, inspections and emergency routes as part of the system. Tent numbers and occupancy change by year, so this record gives no fixed tent total and uses a model demo instead. The demo below estimates tents needed from pilgrims and occupants per tent, the basic logistics arithmetic for a tent city.

title: Arafat Movement Planning
description: Arafat is the plain where pilgrims gather on the Day of Arafat, a central rite of Hajj held in Islamic tradition, and movement planning for Arafat is a problem of moving a very large population in, holding it safely in open ground in summer heat, and moving it out again in a short window toward Muzdalifah. Published planning describes phased arrivals by transport mode, with the metro carrying a large share, buses carrying groups, and foot routes kept separate from vehicle routes, and a plain divided into sectors with services, shade, water and medical posts. The departure from Arafat is the critical movement: a whole population leaving in a few hours, at nightfall, in heat, which is why departure is scheduled in waves and why the transport-flow record models wave timing. This record states the planning structure in general terms; no arrival or departure total is claimed as a verified figure for any particular year, and the religious meaning of the gathering is tradition, separate from the transport engineering. The demo below models wave departure time as people divided by hourly transport capacity, the basic scheduling arithmetic for Arafat.

title: Transport Flow Modeling
description: Transport flow modeling for Mecca's pilgrimage movements combines rail, bus and foot flows into one timed system, because a pilgrimage journey is rarely a single mode: a pilgrim may travel by metro, then walk, then board a bus, and each transfer is a queue as well as a movement. Published modeling approaches include timetable-based rail models, bus-fleet models from fleet size and turnaround time, and pedestrian models from density and width, joined at interchanges where the slowest transfer governs the whole journey. The Mashaaer Metro's published capacity of about 72,000 passengers per hour and the Haramain railway's 417 seats per train are the kinds of published inputs such a model uses, with their dates attached, while bus and foot capacities are modeled from fleet and corridor data. This record's demo is a model, not an operational plan, and a real operational plan would need current timetables, fleet lists and corridor widths, none of which are claimed here. The demo below combines metro, bus and foot hourly capacities into a system total and identifies the smallest mode, which governs the interchange.

title: Bottleneck Analysis
description: A bottleneck is any point where demand exceeds the capacity of the next section, so a queue forms upstream, and bottleneck analysis finds those points before a crowd does. In pilgrimage movements, bottlenecks commonly occur at gates, stairways, escalators, corridor narrowings, ticket and security checks, vehicle-to-foot transfers, and any place where a wide flow meets a narrow exit. Analysis proceeds by listing every section in order, stating its capacity in people per hour from width, speed and density models, and comparing it with the demand arriving from upstream, with the smallest capacity governing the whole route. A bottleneck can also move: clearing one gate can create a queue at the next stairway, so analysis must cover the whole route, not one point. Published crowd-safety guidance treats bottleneck analysis as a design-stage duty, not a post-incident explanation, and this record's demo is a model of that analysis, not a survey of any real route. The demo below lists model section capacities along a route and finds the bottleneck, the section with the smallest capacity.

title: Emergency Evacuation Modeling
description: Emergency evacuation modeling estimates how long it takes a crowd to leave a space through available exits, and it is used to test whether a venue, tent district or station can be cleared before a hazard, such as fire or a structural failure, makes escape impossible. The basic model divides the number of people by the total exit flow, where exit flow is exit width multiplied by flow per metre of width, and then adds detection, alarm and pre-movement time, the time before people start moving, which published models show can exceed movement time itself. Evacuation models must also account for people with reduced mobility, for smoke or heat that closes an exit, and for the fact that crowds do not split evenly across exits unless signage and staff direct them. This record's demo is a model, not an evacuation plan for any real place, and a real plan needs surveyed exit widths, real population counts and drills, none of which are claimed here. Evacuation planning for the holy sites is coordinated with civil-defence authorities. The demo below computes evacuation time as pre-movement time plus people divided by exit flow, the standard textbook form.

title: Heat-and-Crowd Interaction
description: Heat and crowding interact: heat slows walking speed, increases rest stops and water needs, raises the risk of heat illness, and makes a dense crowd harder to move, while a dense crowd makes heat worse by trapping warm air, blocking shade and wind, and delaying access to water, shade and medical help. Published Hajj health planning treats heat as a crowd-safety factor in its own right, with shade, ventilation, water points, misting, scheduling away from peak heat where possible, and medical posts positioned along routes, not only at destinations. The interaction is nonlinear in published models: a crowd that is safe at a moderate temperature can become unsafe at a high temperature at the same density, because speed falls and stops rise, so flow falls and density rises further. This record's demo is a simple illustrative model of that feedback, not a physiological heat model, and it gives no personal medical advice. The environment pair gives the climate background for this interaction. The demo below models speed falling as temperature rises, and flow falling with speed, as an illustration of the heat-crowd feedback.

title: Real-Time Monitoring Systems (General, Published)
description: Real-time monitoring for pilgrimage crowds combines cameras, counting sensors, transport data, weather data and reports from staff on the ground, fused in operations centres that watch density, flow and queue length and can slow entries, open relief routes or redirect groups before a bottleneck becomes dangerous. Published descriptions of Hajj operations describe camera networks, crowd-counting and flow analysis, geographic information systems for sector management, and coordination across transport, health and civil-defence bodies, with decisions communicated to group leaders and transport operators. Monitoring is only a safety system if its warnings reach an operator who can act and if the action is rehearsed: a screen that nobody watches, or a warning with no relief route, is not a safety system. Privacy and data rules for camera and counting systems are a published governance matter, and this record describes monitoring in general functional terms without claiming any particular system's current coverage, accuracy or vendor, none of which is in the public record consulted. The demo below models sensor coverage as monitored area divided by total area, and flags sectors below a stated coverage threshold, the basic monitoring audit.

title: Simulation Methods
description: Simulation methods for crowds range from simple flow models, which treat a crowd as a fluid with density and speed, through cellular and agent models, which give each simulated person rules for speed, spacing and destination, to full-scale exercises and drills, which test a plan with real people at reduced scale. Agent models, notably the social-force model in published literature, let researchers test gate widths, schedules and signage before building, and Monte Carlo simulation, which runs a model many times with varied inputs, shows how sensitive a plan is to a late train, a closed exit or a hotter day. Simulation is only as good as its inputs and its validation: a model fitted to one venue does not automatically describe another, and a model that has never been compared with observed counts is a hypothesis, not evidence. This record's demo uses a fixed random seed, so its output is reproducible, and it is labeled as a simulation, not as an observation of any real crowd. The demo below runs a fixed-seed Monte Carlo model of clearance times and reports the mean and the worst run, showing why a plan must survive its worst run, not its average.

This record's demo uses a fixed random seed, so its output is reproducible, and it is labeled as a simulation, not as an observation of any real crowd. The demo below runs a fixed-seed Monte Carlo model of clearance times and reports the mean and the worst run, showing why a plan must survive its worst run, not its average.

title: Lessons from Past Incidents (Factual, Respectful, Published)
description: Published lessons from past crowd incidents at pilgrimage gatherings and at other large gatherings are stated here in general, respectful terms, without graphic detail and without figures for any individual event. The recurring lessons in published crowd-safety literature are consistent: schedule movements in waves rather than releasing whole populations at once; keep flows one-way and separated at entries, exits and crossings; design structures for the peak flow, not the average; monitor density in real time and act on rising density early, before movement stops; provide relief routes, shade, water and medical access along routes, not only at destinations; and rehearse the plan with all agencies together, because a plan that exists only on paper fails at the first unexpected closure. The Jamarat Bridge redesign and the wave scheduling described in earlier records are published examples of these lessons applied. This record honours those affected by past incidents by stating the lessons plainly and by refusing to treat any incident as a spectacle. title: Capacity Planning Formulas
description: Capacity planning for a crowd space starts from three formulas, all models, that together size a space, a route and a schedule. First, space capacity: area divided by area per person at the chosen safe density, which gives the number of people a space can hold. Second, route capacity: flow per metre of width multiplied by width multiplied by time, which gives the number of people a route can pass in an hour. Third, Little's law for queues: the number of people in a system equals arrival rate multiplied by time in the system, which sizes waiting areas from arrival rates and waiting times. Planning uses safe densities, not maximum densities, and adds margin for heat, reduced mobility and unexpected closures, so a plan that exactly fits its formulas with no margin is treated as fragile. This record's demo applies all three formulas to one model case, so a reader can see how space, route and queue planning join into one capacity plan. The demo below applies space capacity, route capacity and Little's law to model inputs, as a worked capacity plan.

title: Crowd-Safety Glossary
description: This glossary defines the terms used across the crowd-science pair in plain language, so a reader needs no prior crowd-science vocabulary. Density is people per square metre. Flow is people passing a line per unit time, often per metre of width per second. Speed is metres per second. Bottleneck is the section with the smallest capacity on a route. Level of service is a graded scale from free movement to crush conditions, from published pedestrian literature. Pre-movement time is the delay before people start moving after an alarm. Wave scheduling is releasing a population in timed groups rather than all at once. Relief route is an alternative route opened when a main route fills. Safe density is a chosen design density with margin below dangerous densities, not a measured maximum. Each term is a model term: it describes a quantity in a model of crowd behaviour, and using the term correctly means stating its value, its unit and its model, never quoting a number bare. Cross-references point to the record where each term is first modeled. The demo below counts the glossary terms defined here and prints them, as an index check for the pair.
